reason: The run renders the same sense differently in parallel passages: Matt 13:21 has "stumbles" where Mark 4:17 has "fall away"; Matt 13:57 has "stumbled over him" where Mark 6:3 has "took offense at him"; 1 Cor 8:13 has "cause to fall" where the Gospels have "cause to stumble"; John 6:61 has "make you stumble". The departure from the traditional "offend" is sound but applied unevenly, so the register must fix which rendering applies under which condition.
sense: to trip someone up, bringing about their fall in faith or loyalty to God, whether into sin, desertion or rejection; in the passive, to be so tripped up

alternates.when: Passive where the person is tripped up or put off from trust without outright desertion being stated: Matt 11:6 and Luke 7:23 ("stumble because of me"), and 2 Cor 11:29 ("is made to stumble").

Passive where giving up allegiance under pressure is in view: the rootless hearer under persecution (Matt 13:21, Mark 4:17), the many in the last days (Matt 24:10), the disciples deserting on the night of the arrest (Matt 26:31, Matt 26:33, Mark 14:27, Mark 14:29; with the Greek preposition, "fall away because of me"), and John 16:1.

Where the sense is to be affronted, shocked or repelled by a person or saying. Passive "take offense": the Nazareth townspeople at Jesus (Matt 13:57, Mark 6:3) and the Pharisees at his saying (Matt 15:12). Active "give offense": the temple-tax collectors (Matt 17:27).
Romans 14:21 only, where the verb stands beside a different Greek verb that must itself be rendered "stumble", so the two need distinct English.

rationale: The verb comes from the Septuagint's word for a trap or obstacle and means to bring about someone's fall in loyalty to God. "Offend" now suggests hurt feelings, which is too weak, and "cause to sin" is narrower than the Greek. "Cause to stumble" keeps the picture and the breadth, and the run already favours it. In the passive, "fall away" is the clearest English where desertion is meant, and "take offense" remains accurate where people are affronted by Jesus or his words.
standard_view: The KJV has "offend" throughout. Modern versions divide the active between "cause to sin" (ESV, older NIV) and "cause to stumble" (NASB, NIV 2011, NRSV in places). For the passive they commonly use "fall away" for desertion and "take offense" for Nazareth and the Pharisees. Matt 11:6 is split between "take offense at me" and "stumble on account of me", and John 6:61 between "offend" and "cause to stumble". Standard lexicons distinguish causing a fall or sin, with its passive of falling away or being repelled by someone, from the weaker sense of shocking or giving offense.
